newsitem.title: TURKEY: Erbakan under pressure from Turk army meeting.
newsitem.headline: Erbakan under pressure from Turk army meeting.

text.p: Turkey's powerful army has brought forward a key meeting, the defence minister said on Wednesday, in what the media said was an apparent attempt to put pressure on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to clamp down on Islamist activism.
"The High Military Council will meet on May 26," Defence Minister Turhan Tayan told reporters. He said the agenda of the meeting had not been set.

The meeting will take place five days before the monthly gathering of the military-dominated National Security Council, which in February issued demands designed to clamp down on Islamist zeal. Erbakan is due to attend both meetings.
The High Military Council, a twice yearly affair grouping 15 top generals, deals with promotions, retirements and disciplinary issues in its summer meeting.
Tayan also said Ankara was going ahead with plans to hold joint naval exercises with Israel, despite comments by Erbakan suggesting they may be postponed.
"There is no question of such a postponement," he said. "There is no question of the prime minister approving or postponing of his own accord."

Turkish newspapers said the military aimed to make Erbakan, modern Turkey's first islamist leader who has been stalling on the February demands, sign orders for the dismissal of army members deemed to have been involved in Islamist activity.
"Council warning to the Hoja," said Radikal daily, referring to Erbakan by his popular title, meaning "Teacher".
"The Chief of Staff is planning to give the government an extremely strong message by calling the extraordinary council meeting," Sabah daily said in a front-page article.
The Islamist-conservative coalition government is also under threat from dissident MPs and the opposition, who are trying to form an Islamist-free alternative alliance.
Rebel government MP Yalim Erez said on Wednesday he was sure the government would fall.
"The Turkish people no longer accept this government," Erez told Turkey's biggest grouping of businessmen at a meeting. "There is no barrier or suspicion remaining over an alternative government."
Erez said it was now up to the junior coalition partner -- the conservatives of Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller -- to decide on how the government would be replaced.
Unless Ciller agrees to withdraw from the coalition and join the opposition in a new alliance, the dissidents will have to bring down the government with a censure motion.
